Norman Conquest. The invasion and takeover of England by William the Conqueror and his Norman forces occurred between 1066 and the early 1070s. Triggered by a disputed succession to the English throne, the conquest decisively defeated Anglo-Saxon resistance and replaced the English nobility with Norman-French lords. This single military event fundamentally transformed English language, culture, law, and institutional development for centuries to come. The conquest began with William of Normandy's invasion in September 1066, motivated by his claim to the throne of England following the death of Edward the Confessor. The decisive Battle of Hastings took place in October 1066, where William defeated and killed Harold Godwinson, the Anglo-Saxon king, and destroyed the English noble class in a single afternoon. The conquest took several years to consolidate fully. Pockets of Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian resistance persisted, especially in the North, until the early 1070s as William gradually brought all England under Norman control. Norman feudal institutions replaced Anglo-Saxon systems. The Normans introduced the knight, the castle, and the hierarchical feudal structure that defined medieval England for the next several centuries. The Norman victory ended Scandinavian influence over England permanently. It aligned England with France culturally and politically, and tied English succession to Norman dynastic struggles. William commissioned the Domesday Book in 1086, an unprecedented administrative survey that asserted total royal dominion over all English lands and subjects. Norman French became the language of the English court and nobility for centuries. The blending of Norman and Anglo-Saxon cultures eventually produced English identity and the English language itself, creating a hybrid civilization from two distinct peoples.
